title: peered-subnet-dns-fallback-scratchpad
content:
Context:
- Private deployment customer report: intermittent TLS handshake failures when calling outbound partner APIs (~2-5% of requests) from pods in peered-subnets. Only affects peered VPCs (VPC-A <-> VPC-B peering). Hosted (non-peered) workloads unaffected.
- Symptoms: TLS handshake stalls around ServerHello/Certificate (client times out), sometimes immediate TCP RST. App-level errors: "upstream handshake failed: unexpected EOF" and "SSL_read: Connection reset by peer". Latency p50 normal, p95/p99 spikes and error rate visible during some windows.

Initial hypothesis summary (quick notes):
- Asymmetric routing: replies from remote partner might be taking different path that doesn't traverse NAT/IGW expected, causing TCP ACKs to be dropped.
- MTU/MSS fragmentation on route between peered VPCs (VXLAN or transit overlay) causing TLS records to get fragmented and break handshake.
- DNS resolution or DNS64/NAT64 weirdness when peering across accounts/regions.
- Security group / NACL rejecting ephemeral ports on return path (less likely but possible for certain peered subnets).
- AWS VPC peering does NOT support transitive routing; we might have misconfigured route table and traffic to IGW/NAT is asymmetric.

What I tried (commands + outputs / observations):
1) From a failing pod (kubectl exec into app container)
- curl -v --resolve partner.example.com:443:198.51.100.23 https://partner.example.com/health -o /dev/null
  -> hangs at "Connected to partner.example.com" then after ~15s: "OpenSSL SSL_connect: SSL_ERROR_SYSCALL in connection to partner.example.com:443" (errno 104: Connection reset by peer)

- strace -f curl ... (quick look) -> shows socket read returning 0 after sending ClientHello (peer closed).

2) tcpdump on node hosting pod (host NIC) and tcpdump on NAT instance (NAT gateway logs)
- tcpdump: saw outbound SYN, got SYN/ACK back from partner, sent ACK and ClientHello, then no further segments until partner sends RST shortly after.
- NAT gateway flow logs: show established flows but occasional RSTs. No consistent duplication.

3) ip route get and sysctl checks on node
- ip route get 198.51.100.23 -> correct route via peering route table to peered-subnet router.
- sysctl net.ipv4.ip_forward = 1 (expected on NAT hosts)

4) conntrack dump on linux NAT/edge appliance (conntrack -L | grep partner IP)
- Several entries in TIME_WAIT/ESTABLISHED, but a subset shows "ASSURED" then quickly transition to "UNREPLIED" before timeout. Suggests reply path not matching expectation.

5) DNS checks
- dig partner.example.com @10.0.0.2 -> returns both private and public A records depending on resolver. We have split-horizon: peered VPC resolver returns private IP for some clients and public for others.
- curl with --resolve forcing public IP: sometimes works (maybe different egress path).

6) MTU tests
- ping -M do -s 1400 partner-ip -> fragmentation required or no reply? Observed fragmentation for sizes >1420.
- tracepath partner-ip -> reports MTU 1404 on one hop then 1500 on another, inconsistent.

7) iptables / nftables checks on node and NAT appliance
- iptables -t mangle -L PREROUTING -> empty
- iptables -t nat -L POSTROUTING -> MASQUERADE present for pod CIDR when going to IGW, but not for traffic destined to peered VPC. NAT config intentionally avoids masquerading for peered routes—but that could be causing return path asymmetry if partner expects source to be e.g. public IP.
- tcpdump with src-port mapping shows source IPs in peered traffic are pod IPs (not NATed). Partner upstream sometimes rejects pod IPs because they are unknown private range -> might RST.

8) kube-proxy / calico observations
- Calico policies: no egress policy blocking. NAT/masquerade config: ipPool with masquerade set to true only for external CIDR ranges. Calico's iptables rules show no mangle tcpMSS clamping.

Error snippets observed in app logs: (copied raw)
- 2026-03-01T09:12:18.122Z ERROR upstream handshake failed: EOF while reading response body
- 2026-03-01T09:44:03.556Z WARN TLS handshake stalled: client hello sent, no server cert (timeout)
- OpenSSL: "SSL_connect: ssl=0x7f9d7800a680: I/O error during system call" / "Connection reset by peer"

Why MTU could matter here: TLS ClientHello + SNI + extensions can push packet size above path MTU. If some middlebox drops ICMP fragmentation-needed messages or MSS isn't clamped, segments may be dropped and handshake stalls. Also TCP segmentation offload (TSO/GSO) can hide fragmentation symptoms until handshake data is lost.

New hypothesis emerging after experiments:
- For peered-subnet traffic we are not NATing source IPs. partner.example.com occasionally rejects requests from private IPs (RST). Some peered routes go via partner's peered path (direct) while others inadvertently route out to internet (public IP path) causing inconsistent behavior. Essentially mixed egress (sometimes direct, sometimes via NAT/IGW) causing intermittent failures depending on which path the DNS resolution returned and how partner responds.
- Additionally, MTU mismatch amplifies failures for larger TLS handshakes and HTTP/2 multiplexed frames.

Quick reproduction plan (minimal):
- From node: curl --interface <host-interface> --local-port 42000 --resolve partner.example.com:443:198.51.100.23 https://partner.example.com/health -v
- Use two variants: one where we NAT source to public IP (iptables -t nat -A POSTROUTING -s podCIDR -d partnerIP -j MASQUERADE) and one without NAT. See difference in RST rate.
- Run openssl s_client -connect partnerIP:443 -tls1_2 -servername partner.example.com -msg -debug to capture handshake messages and see where it stops.

Short-term mitigations tried / considered:
- Configure iptables POSTROUTING MASQUERADE for peered-subnet->partner-IP to force consistent egress source (did a test on a bastion, reduced failure rate to ~0.5%). Caveat: breaks peering semantics if partner expects original private IPs for auth.
- Add TCPMSS clamp on FORWARD chain: iptables -t mangle -A FORWARD -p tcp --tcp-flags SYN,RST SYN -j TCPMSS --clamp-mss-to-pmtu -> appears to reduce large-packet failures in our synthetic tests.
- Adjust Calico IPPool to masquerade outgoing traffic to specified destination IP ranges. Doing so cluster-wide needs product decision (loss of original source IP visibility).
- Contact partner to allow our pod CIDR in ACLs or accept peered private source ranges.

Notes about DNS split-horizon / resolver behaviour:
- Some clients inside peered VPC are hitting an internal resolver which returns private IPs (direct peering path). Other times (depending on which resolver path used by the app/container) we get public IP which goes via NAT/IGW. This mismatch explains intermittent nature. Need to ensure all pods use consistent resolver behavior (kube-dns config or node resolv.conf pointing).
- We observed that pods using stub resolver via 169.254.169.253 (AWS VPC resolver) get different answers than the node's /etc/resolv.conf DNS caching config.

Action items / next steps (ordered):
1) Short term (owners: Aisha / Ethan)
   - Add temporary iptables MASQUERADE rule on NAT/bastion host for partner IPs and monitor error rate for 12h. Rollback if partner rejects private IPs. (Aisha)
   - Enable TCPMSS clamping on forwarding nodes and on transit hosts. (Ethan)
2) Short/med term (Priya / infra)
   - Sync with partner: confirm whether they accept private source IPs from our peered ranges. If not, decide whether to always NAT egress to partner IPs. (Priya)
   - Standardize DNS resolution: force pods to use node-local DNS cache or a single resolver IP that returns consistent records for partner.example.com. Update CoreDNS configmap and test. (Infra)
3) Medium term (product/infra)
   - Update design doc: peered-vpc egress policy (options: prefer direct peering with source-preservation vs force NAT for peered cross-account integrations). Add guidance for TLS-sensitive workloads and MSS clamping. (Aisha + Product)
   - Add monitoring alert that triggers when handshake failure rates > 0.5% for peered egress to critical partners.
4) Diagnostics to run if it recurs (runbook snippet):
   a) curl with --resolve and openssl s_client to determine whether public vs private IP is used.
   b) tcpdump simultaneously on pod host and NAT/gateway to verify sequence of SYN/SYN-ACK/ACK/ClientHello.
   c) conntrack -L to find entries marked UNREPLIED.
   d) iptables-save / nft list ruleset to check NAT/masq for peered CIDRs.
   e) ping/tracepath for MTU discovery and apply TCPMSS clamp if mismatch found.

Misc scratchpad thoughts / TODO notes:
- Check whether kube-proxy iptables mode is doing any unexpected SNAT for services.
- Verify if AWS Peering across regions has any documented MTU/fragmentation caveats.
- Consider adding small library-level retry/backoff for partner API to hide intermittent handshake failures (short-term app mitigation).
- If we choose to NAT all peered egress to partner IPs, update observability to map source external IP to original pod for auditing (X-Forwarded-For or token-based identification).

Open questions (for discussion):
- Do we prefer preserving source IP over consistent connectivity? Partner auth may rely on source IP, so altering NAT behavior has security/contract implications.
- Should peered route tables include explicit route for partner's public IPs to go via NAT (so public-IP egress consistently NATed) and private IPs go via peering? Can we enforce resolver consistency instead?

Last quick log dump (raw snippets):
- node-02 tcpdump snippet: "12:34:56.789123 IP 10.2.1.45.51234 > 198.51.100.23.443: Flags [S], seq 0, win 64240, options [mss 1460,sackOK,TS val 123456 ecr 0,nop,wscale 7], length 0"
- partner -> "12:34:56.789456 IP 198.51.100.23.443 > 203.0.113.10.51234: Flags [S.], seq 0, ack 1, win 29200, options [mss 1460], length 0"
- after ClientHello sent by us: no server certificate back, then RST: "12:34:57.002511 IP 198.51.100.23.443 > 203.0.113.10.51234: Flags [R], seq 1, win 0, length 0"

If anyone picks this up: start with enabling TCPMSS clamp and forcing consistent resolver for pods. That'll likely cut most of the noise and give time to coordinate NAT/source-IP policy with the partner.

-- Aisha
